item.title: 每天工作2小時就能財富自由？網紅教你「躺賺」自己卻靠賣課致富！AI副業熱潮誰才是真正贏家？【TODAY 看世界】
item.itunes:title: 每天工作2小時就能財富自由？網紅教你「躺賺」自己卻靠賣課致富！AI副業熱潮誰才是真正贏家？【TODAY 看世界】
item.itunes:author: TODAY 看世界
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r9H_HxNlEG8

值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭開社群平台「輕鬆打造被動收入」宣傳背後的真實殘酷現狀與市場飽和困境。
  • 透過 BBC 記者的半年度副業實測數據，具體了解販售數位產品的隱性時間與金錢成本。
  • 深度剖析網紅靠販售「致富課程」與轉售權（MRR）獲利的模式，以及這類手法如何類似於傳統多層次傳銷（MLM）。

摘要

網紅鼓吹的被動收入神話與三大熱門副業

作者指出，近來 Instagram 等社群平台上掀起一股追求被動收入與副業致富的熱潮，相關標籤累積數千萬則貼文，宣傳只要每天花一兩小時用電腦工作，就能月入數十萬。作者歸納了網紅最常推薦的三種賺錢管道：第一種是利用 Canva 等設計工具製作邀請卡、履歷表等數位產品，並在 Etsy 等電商平台上架重複販售；第二種是透過社群分享連結賺取分潤的聯盟行銷；第三種則是利用 AI 工具輔助，在家接案處理上字幕、聽打逐字稿或商品評測等遠端兼職。

BBC 記者親身實測：投入半年倒貼虧損的殘酷真相

為了驗證這些副業是否真能輕鬆獲利，BBC 記者 Vivian 親自展開為期六個月的實測。她嘗試製作派對邀請函模板，卻發現設計耗費大量時間，上架後更扣除各項平台手續費僅剩微薄毛利；想接聽打案子卻因申請者過多而排入候補。整整半年下來，Vivian 僅售出 3 份模板，總營收約新台幣 120 元，各項支出成本卻超過 6,500 元。作者強調，市場上早已充斥超過 560 萬名活躍賣家與上億件商品，在缺乏市場需求與行銷能力的情況下，一般人盲目跟風只會陷入激烈的低價削價競爭。

「教人做副業」才是最賺錢的生意：變相的傳銷套路

作者分析指出，在副業熱潮中真正能大發利市的，往往不是執行副業的人，而是「教別人如何做副業」的網紅。販售單份模板僅能賺取幾十元，但開設線上課程或經營付費諮詢社群卻能收取數千至數萬元的學費。美國更興起名為主轉售權（Master Resell Rights, MRR）的數位課程模式，購買者花錢上課後即可取得將該課程轉賣給下一個人的權利。媒體與專家分析，這種銷售模式本質上與傳統多層次傳銷（MLM）極為相似，網紅販賣的其實並非真正的專業技能，而是一個看似觸手可及的「致富美夢」。

AI 時代的青年生存焦慮與被剝削的美國夢

作者進一步探討人們渴望被動收入背後的結構性原因。許多人投入副業並非想發大財，而是面對就業市場緊縮、物價通膨等經濟壓力下，單靠正職收入難以維持生活。雖然生成式 AI 降低了創業技術門檻，卻也讓內容生產更加氾濫且難以變現。相關調查顯示，絕大多數副業者更渴望的是一份穩定正職。然而，社群上氾濫的成功學故事往往挪用了「美國夢」敘事，將結構性的經濟困境個人化，誤導大眾以為失敗純粹是因為自己不夠努力，讓想改善生活的年輕世代在現實與虛幻之間承擔更多挫敗與損失。

================================================

Let’s all imagine this: you wake up naturally in the morning, make some coffee, scroll through your phone, and occasionally open your laptop to work for an hour or two. The rest of the time, you can binge-watch shows or go out whenever you want. Best of all, even if you do nothing, the money in your bank account just keeps growing. Doesn't that sound like a dream? Recently, a ton of influencers on Instagram have been teaching people how to live this life through passive income and side hustles. As of October, related hashtags on Instagram have. accumulated about 25.6 million posts. Many videos even claim to earn hundreds of thousands of NT dollars per month, suggesting that even stay-at-home moms can easily make money. So, is this passive income really that easy to earn ? Hello everyone, I’m Fan Qi-fei. Welcome to "Fan Qi's View of the World. " Before we continue with today's main story, I have an announcement: with less than a month left until November 28th, have you decided who you’re.

voting for? Next Tuesday at 8 PM, I will invite Xiao-Zhou from "Ren Jia Wen Ben" to do a livestream in the LINE community "Fan's International News Arena." We will discuss some of the more intense mayoral and county magistrate races, such as whether Shen Bo and Su Hui can really change the political landscape in the Twin Cities. If you haven't joined the "Arena" yet, scan this QR code now to join. You can also see what international news everyone is typically interested in. If you have any questions for the candidates, feel free to leave them in the discussion thread. Alright, the ad. is over. Now, on to our main story: how are these influencers actually teaching people to make money? There are a few popular methods. The first is selling digital products. For example, using online design tools like Canva to create wedding invitations, schedules, or resume templates, then selling them on e-commerce platforms like Etsy. Since you're selling digital files, there's no printing or inventory needed —just design once, and every subsequent copy can be sold repeatedly. The second is affiliate marketing using commission links. For instance, if you.

share a great skincare product on social media and include an exclusive purchase link, you get a commission whenever someone places an order through that link. These influencers claim you don't need to produce goods or handle customer service—just share the link. Sounds super simple, right? The third is taking on online freelance gigs. For example, subtitling videos, transcribing audio files, or helping to test and review products. These jobs can all be done from home with the help of AI, so influencers say office workers, homemakers, or even people. without specialized skills can use their spare time to earn extra cash. But are these methods really that lucrative? Vivian, a journalist for the BBC, decided to test this herself, spending six months trying out five different side hustles recommended by influencers. First was selling digital products, but she didn't expect that designing eight party invitations alone would take her eight hours. She discovered halfway through that she had accidentally used paid Canva assets, so she spent another five hours fixing them. Finally, she uploaded the templates, but each only sold for about.

65 NT dollars. After the first sale, and after deducting platform transaction and processing fees, she only netted about 40 dollars. This meant that when factoring in the full month's costs—even without counting one-off electricity bills—she was already losing money. She tried a second method, but after promoting the products, nobody bought them. She wanted to do transcription and subtitling work, but was waitlisted because there were too many applicants. After six months, Vivian had only sold a total of three templates. After deducting transaction fees, her total. income was about 120 NT dollars, but her costs exceeded 6,500 NT dollars. She realized that the "simple side hustles" influencers talk about are actually like learning a whole new profession; you have to know design, understand marketing, and find a way to get customers. Even with Canva and generative AI today, you can quickly create a bunch of products without knowing how to draw or design, but if you can do it, others can too! According to released data, by the end of last year, there were already about 5.6 million active sellers on the.

platform. With over 100 million products, the competition is clearly intense. Economists told the BBC that many of these influencer claims about making a fortune through passive income completely ignore market demand. If everyone follows the tutorials and starts selling the exact same templates , and the number of products keeps growing, who is actually going to buy them? Besides, if selling Canva templates were really that profitable, why wouldn't these influencers just sell the templates themselves instead of spending so much time making videos teaching everyone to compete for. business? That’s because what they are really trying to sell you isn't the templates at all, but rather—The BBC reported on an American mother who actually made money from digital products. She used AI to create product display images for clothing, found other sellers in the market with similar needs, and accumulated about 4.75 million NT dollars in sales over three years. Interestingly, she later also started teaching others how to create digital products. About 300.

people have bought her courses, costing around 4,900 to 8,100 NT dollars each, plus about 155 active students who pay about 620 NT dollars a month to join her private teaching community. So, Business Insider analyzed in April this year that the hottest side hustle on the internet now isn't actually doing those side hustles, but teaching others how to do them; because selling an invitation card might net a few dozen bucks, but selling a course can fetch thousands, plus you can keep selling. membership coaching services. Consumer watchdog groups in the U.S. have discovered that some influencers who used to be involved in multi-level marketing are now selling digital courses called "Master Resell Rights," or MRR. The way it works is you pay to buy a course that teaches you how to make money, while gaining the rights to resell it; then you can use your own Instagram to promote this course and sell it to the next person, who might then resell it further. In the end, is.

everyone really learning how to do business, or just learning how to sell the same course to more people? Doesn't this sound a lot like typical multi-level marketing, or MLM? In Taiwan, we are more familiar with direct sales companies like Amway. According to New York Magazine reporter Bridget Read's analysis, the hallmark of traditional multi-level marketing is that you don't just earn money by selling products, you also recruit friends and family to join as your. downline and earn bonuses from the team's total sales. In other words, you have to not only sell goods but also constantly expand your sales team. This is a bit different from the influencer marketing we just mentioned, because general affiliate marketing, or even MRR reselling rights, aren't necessarily illegal pyramid schemes. What really matters is whether the income comes from real customers buying products, or if you have to rely on constantly recruiting new people to pay in. The reporter we mentioned, Read, feels that the sales pitches used by these influencers are actually very.

similar to old-school MLM; it's just that before, MLM required you to join an organization to help sell products, whereas now, some influencers want you to follow accounts, watch videos, and comment to get "money-making secrets," which then leads you to buy their course. Both have one thing in common: if you succeed, it means the method works; if you fail, it's because you didn't work hard enough. The problem is that once you've paid for the course, the person selling it has already made their money, and whether you profit or not doesn't affect them at all. Therefore, American communication. scholars also told the press that the most similar aspect between these influencers and traditional MLMs is that what they are actually selling is a "get-rich" dream. Speaking of which. Ultimately, more and more people want to pursue side hustles and create passive income, not necessarily to make a quick buck, but because they've started to wonder: can working a regular job really get me the life I want? Especially with the emergence of AI, which makes this question even more complex. On one hand, AI has lowered the barrier to entry for entrepreneurship, but on the other, it.

has also made market competition much more intense. An influencer who sells online courses told Business Insider that during the pandemic, they could earn tens of thousands of dollars a month just by selling templates, but now that people can just ask AI what they want to learn, who would want to pay for it anymore? Ironically, reports show that some young people in the US are starting their own businesses because jobs are becoming harder to find; a global survey also found that 55%of Gen Z have delayed life plans like marriage and having children due to financial pressure. But does everyone really want to start a. business? The US lending platform LendingTree found that 61%of side-hustlers would struggle to make ends meet without this income, yet 69% would prefer a steady job. Reporter Reed suggests that such stories are so prevalent in the US because they exploit people's expectations of the American Dream, telling everyone that no matter their background, anyone has the chance to become a boss and strike it rich. But when opportunities in reality become increasingly limited, these success stories serve another purpose: they make people believe success depends entirely on themselves,.

and if you can't make it, it’s because you didn’t work hard enough. I am an influencer myself and I know many others; I can tell you right now that every successful influencer I know works incredibly hard. Not only are the hours long, but you also need strong resilience; filming has costs and financial pressures. You need all of that, plus one more thing: you also need good luck. So, would you still want to rely on a side hustle to earn passive income? Feel free to leave a comment and chat with us! If you enjoy this program, please share it so more people can see it. You can subscribe to. our official account, and it will push important news and this program to your phone every day. If you happen to miss it, head over to the international channel to find all our reports. Looking at the world from different perspectives, we select one international topic daily to bring you along.

=============

值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭開社群平台「輕鬆打造被動收入」宣傳背後的真實殘酷現狀與市場飽和困境。
  • 透過 BBC 記者的半年度副業實測數據，具體了解販售數位產品的隱性時間與金錢成本。
  • 深度剖析網紅靠販售「致富課程」與轉售權（MRR）獲利的模式，以及這類手法如何類似於傳統多層次傳銷（MLM）。

摘要

網紅鼓吹的被動收入神話與三大熱門副業

作者指出，近來 Instagram 等社群平台上掀起一股追求被動收入與副業致富的熱潮，相關標籤累積數千萬則貼文，宣傳只要每天花一兩小時用電腦工作，就能月入數十萬。作者歸納了網紅最常推薦的三種賺錢管道：第一種是利用 Canva 等設計工具製作邀請卡、履歷表等數位產品，並在 Etsy 等電商平台上架重複販售；第二種是透過社群分享連結賺取分潤的聯盟行銷；第三種則是利用 AI 工具輔助，在家接案處理上字幕、聽打逐字稿或商品評測等遠端兼職。

BBC 記者親身實測：投入半年倒貼虧損的殘酷真相

為了驗證這些副業是否真能輕鬆獲利，BBC 記者 Vivian 親自展開為期六個月的實測。她嘗試製作派對邀請函模板，卻發現設計耗費大量時間，上架後更扣除各項平台手續費僅剩微薄毛利；想接聽打案子卻因申請者過多而排入候補。整整半年下來，Vivian 僅售出 3 份模板，總營收約新台幣 120 元，各項支出成本卻超過 6,500 元。作者強調，市場上早已充斥超過 560 萬名活躍賣家與上億件商品，在缺乏市場需求與行銷能力的情況下，一般人盲目跟風只會陷入激烈的低價削價競爭。

「教人做副業」才是最賺錢的生意：變相的傳銷套路

作者分析指出，在副業熱潮中真正能大發利市的，往往不是執行副業的人，而是「教別人如何做副業」的網紅。販售單份模板僅能賺取幾十元，但開設線上課程或經營付費諮詢社群卻能收取數千至數萬元的學費。美國更興起名為主轉售權（Master Resell Rights, MRR）的數位課程模式，購買者花錢上課後即可取得將該課程轉賣給下一個人的權利。媒體與專家分析，這種銷售模式本質上與傳統多層次傳銷（MLM）極為相似，網紅販賣的其實並非真正的專業技能，而是一個看似觸手可及的「致富美夢」。

AI 時代的青年生存焦慮與被剝削的美國夢
